subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last night in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates an exchange took place between the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) and some hon. members which has implications for the rights and responsibilities of all hon. members. When the minister was questioned about the communications branch of the National Research Council, he told the committee that this agency, which has security responsibilities, had been transferred to the Department of National Defence. When asked what changes in the estimates this necessitated, the minister said:

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Under what particular item it appears in the Department of National Defence I do not know.

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Could I ask you where the change is this year? Where was it last year in the estimates? What vote was it?
MR. Drury: I would hope it would have appeared in a number of votes.

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
You would hope that it would have appeared in a number of votes?
MR Drury: As is customary in security matters.
This was later elaborated upon as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
I would not like to convey the impression that the estimates are inaccurate; that the estimates are dishonest. What I was merely endeavouring to say is that the estimates, the appropriations made for security purposes within the government are recorded in the estimates in a way which would make it difficult for somebody who is hostile or antagonistic to Canada to-
MR Clark (Rocky Mountain): Such as the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
He said that, not me... who are hostile to Canada, through an analysis of the estimates to get some notion of the size, shape and perhaps even the activities of our counter-subversive forces.
Mr. Speaker, the manner in which the government has chosen to deal with secret information is offensive to a democratic system based on the approval of the spending program by an elected assembly. It is insulting to suggest that the choice in a parliamentary system is either to deny and hide the existence of security activities, on the one hand, or to run the risk of exposing totally material which ought to be classified in the national interest. There is a middle ground which is compatible with the parliamentary control of expenditure. The present method is contrary to the Constitution and to the government's own description of the purposes of the estimates. Section 54 of the British North America Act states that the Governor General recommends expenditures to the House for specific purposes. This provision is repeated in Standing Order 62(1) of this House which states:
This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message from the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.
Standing Order 63 is germane to the point, and says in part:
-it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the
Senate.
The emphasis is on the right of the House to approve the details of expenditure. These Standing Orders are further developed by Beauchesne, citations 244(3) and 246(3) which stress that amendments to change financial recommendations of the Crown can only be made after further recommendations by the Crown setting out a new proposal. When the government presents its estimates it states categorically that their purpose is to provide to the House the necessary information on which to make a judgment. In the preface to the estimates for 1975-76, paragraph No. 1, we find this statement:
The proposals with respect to voted items are conveyed formally in these estimates in the wording and amount of the votes which, when included in appropriation acts, become the governing conditions under which the expenditures may be made.
Paragraph 4 continues, in describing reasons for changes in the form of estimates:
The decision of the Government of Canada to adopt a system of budgeting by programs, a "planning, programming, budgeting system", with its emphasis on defining program objectives and showing the full costs for each program, was also a determining factor.
In view of the attitude of the Minister of Science and Technology, these two descriptions are untrue and the assurances they are meant to convey to members of parliament are misleading and deceptive.
I have not raised this question of privilege today, and the matter was not pursued by my colleagues on the miscellaneous estimates committee because we believe that the state has no right to be extremely careful in its release of information considered prejudicial to the security of the state. Quite the contrary: members of this party concerned about freedom of information, such as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), have repeatedly stressed that this is a valid criterion. However, the position which has been taken by the minister represents an unhealthy extreme. Members are to find out about security organizations by accident and then be denied any opportunity to ask questions about the scope and purpose of such activities or the amount of money to be spent on them.
While it would be comforting to be able to accept assurances that everything being done in the name of security and secrecy is fit and proper, recent history is crowded

March 25, 1975
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
with instances of the abuse of security organizations in countries where these organizations were completely shielded from investigation by democratically elected representatives of the people. My proposition with respect to this is that too much security and secrecy brings its own dangers.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this practice referred to by the minister rejects the very procedural foundation upon which approval of estimates is based and prevents members of parliament from fulfilling their responsibilities. For this reason, if you find that I have a prima facie question of privilege I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark):
That the practice of hiding security program estimates amongst unrelated headings be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, and that the committee be empowered to recommend a more suitable procedure for presenting and dealing with estimates relating to national security.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I am the one who has given rise to this question of privilege, perhaps I might say a word on it. Without question, what the hon. gentleman read in the way of citations and instructions governing the preparation and presentation of estimates was entirely factual and covers generally the fullest and most complete disclosure to a responsible parliament that we can contrive. Indeed, in so far as I have been responsible for the preparation and presentation of estimates, that has been the objective I have sought to achieve. However, matters of national security are somewhat different and the problem is not peculiar to Canada; indeed, this is the universal dilemma of the nation state.
In order for a national security program to be effective, it must be prepared to counter undercover, hidden, clandestine operations of other people, such as the intelligent services which operate against the interests of the national state, or against the interest of Canada. The counter-intelligence movement, or the security apparatus which is countering interests whjch are inimical to Canada, or countering interests which are pursuing purposes which are inimical to Canada, must, in order to be effective, itself be under cover and not known to an enemy. To take a popular analogy, this is a bit like engaging in a poker game in which one man discloses his hand by putting it on the table and the other keeps his hidden and then proceeds to bet.
This, however, presents those in a democracy with a serious dilemma, namely, how to have an effective counter-subversive organization which, in order to be effective, must not be publicly known and the operational details of which should not be disclosed to persons against whom it is operating.

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: And the details of which must not be scrutinized by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: I point out to hon. members that the security apparatus of Canada is not directed against Canada; it is directed against those outside Canada whose interests may at times be inimical to our own.

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: That is exactly what Hoover said about the CIA.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: In order to secure funds for these operations, we must and should seek the approval of parliament. The matter must, therefore, be included in the estimates. The problem, from the administrative point of view, is how-

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: To hide it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
-to seek this parliamentary approval without disclosing in a comprehensible and clear way precisely what is being done, and how. In order to achieve this purpose, an endeavour is made not to include in the estimates, as normally is the case with other programs, a discrete heading showing the entire amount of effort, or the entire number of people and the entire organization and purposes involved in counter-subversive operations: these are not put under one heading as by doing so we would serve the cause to which the organization is opposed. To do so would serve them admirably but it would not help Canadians and our parliamentarians.
To get over this dilemma, when members of the House or the House collectively have felt in the past they must know either the global arrangements or the details of the program, we have, on matters involving national security arrangements, informed parliament in camera rather than on a public basis. Members who participate in such in-camera sessions are under the obligation not to use the information they acquire in a public sense, that is, not to use the information they acquire in public ways or in connection with any other program.
I suggest this with some deference, but if it is the view of the House that it is important at this juncture to have information and a briefing on the security arrangements, I would be quite prepared to recommend to my colleague the House leader that arrangements be made for an in-camera session, on the understanding that those who participate in it accept the responsibility for treating in confidence the information they gather in respect of this national problem. They would be obligated not to disclose this in a way which would harm the interests of Canada.
I think this procedure has always been open. I feel strongly that it would not be in the interests of Canada to tip our hand, so to speak, in a public way merely to satisfy curiosity or the demands of those who would write interesting and perhaps exciting articles.

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words on this matter. I noted with interest the reference made by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) to in-camera sessions. The last in-camera session of this House of Commons that I can remember took place in 1944. Therefore, we are talking about something that does not happen under normal conditions.
The other point I want to make is this. It is open to the government, certainly under the Regulations Act and maybe in other ways, to provide that certain matters be kept secret. I suggest that it is one thing for the government to act under that authority if it feels justified in doing so. However, it is quite a different matter to distrib-
March 25, 1975

ute expenditure items through a number of estimates, in effect to distort the picture that is being given to parliament of how money is being spent.

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: I gather it is that practice about which the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) is complaining. I believe the complaint is well taken. If the government wants to keep certain information secret, it should do it legally under the appropriate act; it should not distort the estimates it places before parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the offer that has been made by the minister, I ask that my question of privilege be stood at this time, and perhaps we can discuss the matter further.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-METHOD OF DEALING WITH SECURITY PROGRAMS IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: I might inform the hon. member that I had that very intention, for two reasons. First, the question of privilege raises the very important point of the right of opposition members to be able to make inquiries in an examination of the estimates and in voting supply, as opposed to the right of the government to retain certain information as secret and confidential and to perhaps go to the length of distributing it throughout the estimates in some unseen way in order to protect that secrecy. The question is extremely important and complex, and I would like to look at it carefully. In addition, there is the offer by the minister that might want to be considered by hon. members before this matter is resolved. Accordingly, it would perhaps be best to ruminate over the Easter break and see what might develop.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise to seek permission to move a motion concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. This urgent and pressing matter is the ongoing process of building the Pickering airport, bearing in mind the recent statement made to the House by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) that he would stop this process if it were proven to him that the majority of the people in Toronto were opposed to it. Yesterday, a poll indicated that 54.4 per cent of the people of that city were against the construction of the Pickering airport as the project now stands. Therefore, on the basis of this and previous polls, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That this House instruct the Minister of Transport that the Pickering project be not proceeded with for at least two years in order to enable a continuation of studies concerning this matter, including studies relating to new technology dealing with the reduction of noise levels as well as the possible development of the Toronto Island airport in regard to short-range STOL routes.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST VETERANS IN OBTAINING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House of the decision reached by the government concerning the provision of housing assistance to veterans. As hon. members

March 25, 1975
Veterans' Housing
will recall, and as reported at page 1072 of Hansard for November 5, 1974, I stated that an urban housing program for veterans retiring from post-war careers would be inconsistent with the Veterans Land Act which was an agriculturally-oriented rehabilitation program designed to assist veterans following their discharge from wartime active service.
I went on to say, however, that it was realized many low or modest income veterans have needs in respect of housing, and that in recognition of such awareness and of the greater relevancy of the provisions of the National Housing Act to their needs, a study was under way to examine whether special arrangements should be made to assist these veterans. My colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), shares my pleasure in informing the House that the government has decided to provide some special assistance to low or modest income veterans within the context of the provisions of the National Housing Act.
Having regard for the increasing age of veterans, good housing at low rental levels is economically and physically more practical for many than home ownership. Accordingly, to provide further incentive toward increasing the availability of such accommodation it has been decided to provide an additional capital grant of 10 per cent to nonprofit organizations which build low-rental projects primarily but not necessarily exclusively for the housing of veterans.
As hon. members are aware, there is provision under section 15.1 of the National Housing Act to provide nonprofit organizations with start-up funds of $10,000. A grant or contribution is made of 10 per cent of the capital cost of the building project. Other provisions of the National Housing Act may also be utilized in the development of. section 15.1 projects. Loans equivalent to 100 per cent of the net cost are made on a long term, 50-year basis at a preferential rate of interest.
The additional 10 per cent-which will also be available where the land is acquired by CMHC and leased to the non-profit organization-should be of significant help in the level of rental rates which are established and maintained with respect to projects developed primarily but not necessarily exclusively for veterans. Veterans' associations and other non-profit organizations have shown interest in past years in low rental projects. It is hoped that the provision of an additional 10 per cent capital grant will encourage further or fresh initiatives by such groups.
Turning now to the area of home ownership, the government considers it appropriate to provide a cash subsidy of up to $600 annually to veterans as defined in the Veterans Land Act who obtain loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or from approved lenders for the construction or purchase of new houses and who meet the income and child dependency criteria of the Assisted Home Ownership Program.
This subsidy of up to $600 will be additional to that available under the AHOP plan for the purpose of reducing payments of principal, interest and taxes to the range of 22-25 per cent of a veteran's adjusted income. It will provide a basis, accordingly, for enabling additional veter-
[Mr. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans
ans in the low or modest income levels to acquire home ownership who may not be able to do so today despite the existing favourable provisions of the AHOP plan.
I referred earlier to the advancing years of veterans, and while this does not necessarily have any bearing on their productive capabilities it is only natural that progressively fewer meet the child dependency requirement of the AHOP plan. It is evident, too, that many veterans eligible under AHOP from an income level standpoint would find it more practical and economical-particularly in communities located outside major metropolitan areas-to purchase existing good quality houses rather than build or buy a new one.
In recognition of veterans in these circumstances, an annual interest reduction grant of up to $600 will be made to veterans as defined in the Veterans Land Act who obtain NHA loans from approved lenders, who have not owned a home in the preceding three years and who would be eligible under the AHOP plan except for the child dependency or new house requirements.
I have no intention of suggesting that the special housing assistance measures on behalf of veterans that I have just announced touch on all the needs or circumstances that veterans may have with respect to housing. I would point out, however, that the provisions of the National Housing Act are broad and favourable, and there are a variety of plans in operation in most provinces, many of them in conjunction with the National Housing Act. Even if it were otherwise feasible and possible, therefore, it is not considered that special assistance for veterans would be warranted with respect to each type of requirement they might have and regardless of income level.
It is contemplated that the administration of the measures I have announced will be carried out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with support from officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Similarly, the additional funding required for subsidy purposes will be disbursed by CMHC from resources provided by Veterans Affairs. Not all of the administrative and financial requirements have yet been completed. However, I hope all necessary arrangements will be concluded soon in order that action to implement the measures may be initiated at the earliest possible date.
Earlier in my statement I referred to the Veterans Land Act. Operations under that statute commenced as early as 1942 and this weekend, after more than 30 years of activity, the authority for the director to accept loan applications for the establishment of qualified veterans will come to an end. This does not mean that the act or the administration will cease to exist. More than 140,000 veterans have received financial assistance totalling more than $1 Vi million. Of those veterans, more than 60,000 still have VLA contracts representing a principal indebtedness of $545 million. The contracts for many will not expire until on or about the year 2000, and they will be eligible, of course, to apply for additional loans until March 31, 1977.
The special housing assistance measures for veterans that I have announced do not represent a replacement of the Veterans Land Act because, as I stated previously, it was neither designed nor intended as a housing program but as an agriculturally-oriented, post-war rehabilitation plan. I nevertheless thought it appropriate, Mr. Speaker, to
March 25, 1975

conclude my statement with a brief reference to some of the vital statistics pertaining to VLA operations, to the tremendous contributions the legislation and VLA settlers have made to the growth and well-being of Canada, and to salute the dedicated officials who have administered the act over the years and will continue to do so for many years to come.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST VETERANS IN OBTAINING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me say a word of appreciation to the minister for providing the opposition with a copy of the statement which he just read to the House. Normally it would fall upon the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) to speak for the official opposition on matters related to veterans affairs. However, it may not be known to the House that just this past weekend the hon. member lost his wife who passed away quite suddenly. I know hon. members on all sides of the House will join with me in offering to him and his family our deepest sympathy in their time of bereavement.
I welcome the fact that at long last the minister has seen fit to make a statement regarding housing for veterans. Ever since a few years ago when we saw the Veterans Land Act coming to an end, we on this side of the House, joined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), have made representations on many occasions and used many devices of procedure in the House of Commons to extend the Veterans Land Act in order to accommodate veterans who have not yet been able to provide themselves with proper housing. We were assured at one point when the government defeated our motion to extend the Veterans Land Act that housing legislation was in the works and would soon be presented.
Since then we have been waiting a long time, and that is why we welcome this announcement today. However, I must say we are deeply disappointed with the contents of the announcement, because we were given to understand that special housing legislation would be introduced into the House designed solely for the benefit of veterans and directed toward those people who have given their all in defence of our country in times of great danger and need. But what do we have in the statement made by the minister? We have an embellishment and enlargement of the National Housing Act, really nothing that is pointed directly at the veterans.
These are men who have pride, Mr. Speaker, They took pride in the service they gave their country, and they like to feel that their government and the Parliament of Canada respect them to the point where they will introduce legislation directed specially at them in recognition of their great sacrifice. We feel that despite the amendments to the National Housing Act which the minister referred to, this is really a token gesture to our veterans that is far, far less than we were given to understand the government was going to make in its proposed legislation.
At least twice in his statement the minister said "primarily but not necessarily exclusively for the veterans". We take exception to this. We think these measures should be primarily for the veterans; the veterans are what the Veterans Land Act is all about. We are given to understand that this replaces the Veterans Land Act. We note, too, that some of the increased grants and assistance
Veterans' Housing
to veterans is not being given directly to them but, rather, to non-profit organizations which construct low rental housing projects for people such as veterans but not necessarily for them.
We welcome the fact that the minister has seen fit to propose an amendment that will give a cash subsidy of $600 annually to veterans. This is an important step and it is fitting, proper and right that it should be done. We feel this will help veterans in the low income group. I note that the minister says it is in addition to that available under AHOP, so I presume it is in addition to the $500 already available to people who build or purchase new homes under the National Housing Act or through CMHC. Our principal disappointment with this is that it is not special legislation. I realize the minister has just said that the program does not touch on all the needs or the circumstances veterans may face in respect of housing. This is exactly the fault we find with it; it certainly does not touch on all the needs, and this is again why I say that special legislation should have been introduced.
Much of the work is to be carried out by CMHC with the assistance of the Department of Veterans Affairs. This department has been relegated to second place in the administration of legislation and changes which affect veterans. The department should be in first place because, after all, we are dealing with veterans of our country.
In conclusion, I certainly join with the minister in his salute to the dedicated officials of the department who have over the years administered the Veterans Land Act to the benefit of a great many veterans who chose to settle on the land and become full-time farmers. Too much good cannot be said about the work they have done. However, I register deep disappointment over the fact that we are not seeing today the introduction of a special housing act aimed solely at the needs of our veterans.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST VETERANS IN OBTAINING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with my friend, the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles), in saying how deeply sorry my colleagues and I feel for our friend, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). He is one of the most distinguished and best respected members of this House and we are indeed sorry that he is experiencing this very sad bereavement.
I also join with the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand in expressing, with the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), a word of appreciation for what has been done during the past 30 years or more under the Veterans Land Act. The tribute to those who have administered this legislation is well deserved. I think we should also pay tribute to the veterans who have taken advantage of this legislation and have made Canada a better place for what they have done under its provisions.
In the same friendly mood I should like to say that all of us in this House have a great deal of respect for the able and gallant Minister of Veterans Affairs. When he rises to make an announcement or say anything, our instinct is to approve and applaud. I regret that there has to be some qualification in what I say in that respect today. We feel that this announcement, promised last November 5 and 6,

March 25, 1975
Veterans' Housing
is a very real disappointment. May I point out that in the past 30 years or more, veterans in need of housing or with housing problems have been able to go to the veterans land administration, a division of their own Department of Veterans Affairs. From now on they will go to to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or to the developers who operate under AHOP. There is no longer any special place, a place of their own, for veterans to go, as veterans, to get assistance in connection with their housing needs.
I would also point out that although we have dared to hope during the months that we would be getting legislation respecting veterans housing, there is no suggestion in this announcement that there is to be any legislation at all. By the process of an announcement, veterans are being turned over to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) in this regard. Considering the difficulty that Canadians generally have in getting assistance on their housing problems from that minister, I do not see that this is any great day for veterans-to be told that they must go and see the Minister of State for Urban Affairs or one of the agencies which operate under that minister.
Let me also point out that the statement which, of course, is made today to keep a promise that something would be said before March 31 contains very few details. There was even a comment in the statement to the effect that most of the details have not yet been worked out. All of that leaves open the question of whether there is to be any legislation, and are we going to get any chance of making sure that the provisions which are to be put into play for veterans are really the kind that will be of assistance to them? Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that to us the statement is a disappointment.
In the main, the minister breaks his announcement into two parts; he talks about rental housing for veterans and then about home ownership. Under the heading of rental housing he says that non-profit organizations which can now get grants of a certain size for the construction of rental housing can get an additional 10 per cent if the projects are built primarily, but not necessarily exclusively, for veterans. The most the minister can say in respect of that arrangement is that it should be of significant help in the level of rental rates which are established for such veterans. There is no guarantee at all that there is to be any discernible benefit to veterans. The veteran will just have to go to a non-profit organization, hoping there is one in his area, to try to rent accommodation, daring to hope that the rent will be a little less than it would have been had this announcement not been put into effect. It seems to me to be a very small offer that is being made to veterans so far as rental housing is concerned.
In connection with home ownership, again the veteran is being told he can no longer knock on the door of the Department of Veterans Affairs but must knock on the door of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. He is told there are some additional grants available to help cope with interest, provided he meets all the conditions. First of all he has to be a veteran within the meaning of the definition in the Veterans Land Act, and that in itself is a limitation. Then he has to meet various conditions set down in the National Housing Act or under AHOP. In the final analysis, it means that the veteran who is seeking to buy a home is at the mercy of the developer who operates

under AHOP, and it has been made clear that in recent years there have been practically no homes offered under AHOP in the large urban centres in Canada where 75 per cent of Canadian people live. If no homes are available, the extra assistance is of no help.
There is a slight improvement in that there will be there grants of so much money per year to help a few veterans pay the interest on the mortgage, but of what use is that help if the veteran cannot get a home under AHOP in one of our large cities?
The one thing there is in this program that does not seem to be there for non-veterans is that there can be assistance for the purchase of a home that is already in existence. But, of course, then we are under the various ceilings and provisions that are in the legislation. The cost of a home in our cities is such that one wonders whether it will be of any help.
All told, there is no doubt in my mind that the minister's heart is in the right place and that he wants to help the veterans, but I think he has been conned by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs into making a statement that sounds as though it provides something for veterans but that really provides very little.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to join the two speakers who preceded me in offering the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) our deepest sympathy in his cruel bereavement.
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the statement of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). I listened attentively when he read it and I seriously pondered on the standards of living, the benefits that are granted to veterans in the various countries I had the opportunity of visiting. I thought that Canada, and I am most convinced of this, is one of the countries which have done the most in the last few years to help well deserving veterans.
So, I should like in their name to thank the minister for his statement which will certainly be of assistance to retired veterans. It is obvious that because of their age many of them who would like to own their house are not
March 25, 1975

in a position to keep it as they would like to. To overcome those difficulties, the minister announced that he wants nonetheless to help them provide for themselves decent housing and to this end, an additional capital grant of 10 per cent will be provided to non profit organizations; the program will be under the responsibility of another department.
I would like, and we have to take things as they are, to ask the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), since he will be in charge of the management of that program, to suggest to his officials as well as to those of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to be considerate to veterans, to be patient enough and give them explanations when they will request information on the advantages of the law and those available from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In short, they should not be too harsh with them, rejecting their request on all kinds of pretexts under some regulations which sometimes are not acceptable to the minister or the legislators so as to give further satisfaction and additional advantages to some groups of individuals.
I should also like to ask him, seeing I have had the opportunity of visiting some of the construction done under the supervision of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, whether he is aware that it is not always of the best quality. Veterans have the right to live in comfortable, well-built first quality and solid homes, in which they will be happy to live.
The minister also stated that there will be a cash subsidy of $50 a month. To my mind, that is an excellent idea, a step in the right direction; I am sure that measure will.be welcomed by those who will want to take advantage of it.
There is another aspect of the statement of the minister that I consider very important because I live in a rural area. Provision is made to allow veterans to buy old houses that are still in good condition and can be renovated; this means that the price of these houses will correspond to their means. In addition, in some parishes, on the outskirts of Quebec City or Levis, and the same must surely apply to Montreal and other large cities, several farms have been regrouped, houses have been abandoned which could still be lived in. So, if under the terms of this act veterans are allowed to retire some distance from the cities, in the country, some balance will result between the rural and urban populations; those who live in the country will be able to share the burden of public expenses with a larger number of people. To my mind, because of this, people will be able to say toward the end of their lives: We now live in a healthy environment, where the air is pure, where there is space. That will be the crowning glory of their lives. That way, Canadians will prove their gratitude to them for their devotion and courage in fighting for our freedoms.

Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-46, An Act to amend the National Housing Act, be amended in clause 5:
(a)	by striking out line 49 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"as the corporation may approve and except on the condition that the rental agreement as established between the corporation and the original owner remains in effect for the full term."

(d)	the rental housing project shall be maintained at such standards as the corporation may prescribe in respect thereof; and

He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment we are proposing is an amendment to clause five of the bill. The amendment which the government has proposed to the National Housing Act as set forth in Bill C-46 is outlined in the explanatory note which reads:
4464

National Housing Act
This amendment will enable the corporation to make contributions to owners of rental housing projects who have obtained loans from approved lenders if the owners have entered into agreement with the corporation under which they have agreed to comply with certain conditions relating to the operation of rental housing projects.
This clause refers to limited dividend builders. The purpose the government has in mind is to give subsidies directly to the builders of limited dividend housing. Mr. Speaker, may I go over with you the history of limited dividend housing across the country? For many years very little use was made by builders of the limited dividend housing provision. In recent years, more especially in the last two years, the government, recognizing a shortage of housing, has attempted to use the limited dividend provision of the National Housing Act as a means of persuading builders to build more homes. The amendment it proposes is, in effect, a direct appeal to the builders to build more homes under the limited dividend provision. The attraction offered to the builders is a direct subsidy provided they apply for a loan from an approved lender.
The history of limited dividend building has been a dismal one. In the past, very few houses have been built, and none would be built in the future were it not for the subsidies the minister is prepared to make available. This is the first time I have heard of a minister giving subsidies to builders-one would almost think these builders were living in a welfare state because of their poverty at this time. But, Mr. Speaker, the builders have never had it so good from the point of view of profits. The minister, who has been caught in possession of a very poor record with regard to housing starts, especially in the first three months of this year, is now bringing forward this amendment in order to encourage the contractors to build under this section. However, this is only on the basis that they are given a direct subsidy.
What really hurts is that the people who benefit from the subsidy are not the people who become the tenants in these developments. The people who benefit most are builders. It strikes me that if we are going to attack the problem of housing starts in Canada and try to solve the housing problem of low income people, then we have to take measures to protect this low income group, not only in the number of housing starts but also in the rent to be paid.
This is a very poor approach to solving the housing problem of low income people. The proper approach is to increase the amount of public housing in Canada, as a first step. The second step is to increase the amount of nonprofit housing. The approach of the minister, in keeping with the philosophy of his party, is to give most of the benefits to the builders, so that the "haves" then have more.

For the benefit of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) I am talking to the first motion. I am talking about the limited dividend developers who are being given a direct subsidy by the government so as to encourage them to build more homes. This is what we are opposing. The reason we oppose it is that builders under limited dividend projects enter into agreements with CMHC in regard to rentals for certain periods, usually 5, 10 or 15 years. I would not have some of the qualms I am now expressing if the agreement were for 15 years, but the practice has been, and I am sure will continue to be, to enter into an agreement for only five years.
Let me just draw a picture of the benefits that the developers get in this regard. First of all, they get direct subsidies on the interest paid on mortgages from approved lenders. This brings down the mortgage rate substantially. I suppose the answer of the minister will be that this is reflected in the rent charged the tenant. If this were the case, I would not feel too badly about it. But according to past experience, after the five-year period expires, the owner, who is the builder or developer, has the right to change the agreement. If he does so, the rents of the people in the complex, the apartment building, are changed. If they do not like it-and this has been the history of developers-the developers sell the building. They carve up the building into condominium apartments and then they sell it.
The builder who has received the subsidy on the mortgage from CMHC then sells these condominium apartments and makes a capital gain. That is the first great advantage that he gets. In the meantime, if he has lost any moneys he can claim capital cost allowance, and this capital cost allowance can be applied against any other income the builder may have. Experience has shown that when the building is vested in the owner, the developer, the building standards diminish substantially. There is no control over the building standards, as is the case when CMHC has control.
In addition to that, this is an inefficient use of scarce capital that the government has for housing construction. My authority for that is not only my party but the Canadian Council on Social Development. All the government need do is to get the Bank of Canada to underwrite a bond issue for $1 billion, pay institutions or private investors interest of, say, 9 per cent, and then use this money directly for the building of homes in the public housing sector, in the co-operative sector and in the non-profit sector. But no, the government would rather give money put up by the taxpayers of Canada to builders who are already making a large amount of money.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that I said that the agreements that are entered into are usually for a period of five years. I also said as a result of experience we have learned that the building standards imposed by the builders cannot be equated with those imposed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The minister has put forward an amendment to try to bring these standards up to the standards of Central Mortgage and Housing Corpora-
March 25. 1975	COMMONS DEBATES	4465
tion, but we are still not prepared to accept the measure of control that CMHC is going to impose upon these builders to whom the minister has got down on bended knees and asked to build homes.
We want CMHC to impose standards that will ensure that these homes will be structurally sound for a good length of time. We want CMHC not to enter into a five-year term, giving the full benefit to the owners and developers after that period; we want the term to be 25 years so that a real measure of benefit will be passed on to the tenants, not to the owners.
It is bad enough that the minister is giving a subsidy to the builders. Not only that, but the mortgage insurance on these buildings will not be under the control of CMHC but will be passed over to the private sector. In other words, you have a situation where there is a real rip-off in regard to capital cost allowance. A subsidy is paid to the builder. There is no control over building standards. There is the possibility of a capital gain on the part of the builder after five years when the apartments are turned into condominiums and the people for whom the apartments were intended are driven out. You have inefficient use by the government of scare capital for housing for low and moderate income families. Lastly, mortgage insurance is passed from the public sector, that is CMHC, to the private sector, the insurance companies. Is it any wonder that we in the New Democratic Party feel there should be some guarantees given to tenants in regard to building conditions? Hence the first part of my amendment.
The second part of the amendment provides that CMHC should see to it that such standards as the corporation may prescribe in respect thereof are maintained. In order to put real teeth into this provision, if there is a breach of the conditions on the part of the builders the ownership of the property should pass directly back to CMHC. That is the only effective way of making the builder conform with proper building standards. Giving a builder the right after five years to turn the apartments into condominiums and sell the building at a capital gain is really too much. Rather than five years we say the period of agreement should be 25 years, and then the direct benefit of the subsidy will pass to the tenants.
I should close my argument on this part by pointing out that the limited dividend section has been used by the minister to advance housing primarily for middle income families, and this does little or nothing to provide a solution to the problem in respect of people of low income families.
I remember a speech by the minister to the Toronto Home Builders Association on December 3. At that time he expressed his concern by saying that almost 800,000 Canadian households spent more than 25 per cent of their gross income on shelter. He said what was even more disturbing was the knowledge that 107,000 tenant families with incomes under $3,000 spent over 50 per cent of their incomes for shelter. I am positive that this limited dividend section will do nothing for the 107,000 families who have incomes of under $3,000 and spend 50 per cent of their incomes for shelter.
29557 -8V2
National Housing Act
I am in direct opposition to the philosophy of the minister who wants to pass on the benefits to the builders and developers rather than to encourage and help people in the low income group. It is rather striking that in the brief presented by the Ontario Welfare Council, which has been distributed to all hon. members, it is pointed out that the main target of the limited dividend section is primarily the middle income families. It suggests this is a rental program for middle income families which does nothing for the lower income group.
Surely, at a time when the minister is so concerned about the poor housing record for the first three months of this year, and when his 210,000 target is diminishing every month, he should be directing his attention to the public housing and non-profit sectors. For the minister and this government to give subsidies at this time to builders in order to encourage them to build more homes for middle income families is highly improper. For those reasons we have moved this amendment and have asked for the cooperation of members on both sides. We want the minister to change those aspects in respect of housing standards, and more especially to change the term with regard to the rental agreement from five years to at least 25 years so the benefits in housing may be passed on to the proper persons.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand and share the hon. member's concern about those who are spending a disproportionate share of their income on housing, including those with whom we are dealing and will continue to deal under our non-profit program, our co-operative program, our public housing program, our senior citizens program, and our AHOP program, to which an extension was announced recently.
I do not know whether the hon. member appreciates the purpose of this particular legislation, but it is intended to deal with what is emerging as the most critical single issue in the housing situation in Canada, and which affects people not actually in the poverty group, as we say, but Canadians on low incomes who are finding it impossible to find accommodation without spending a disproportionate amount of their income on rent. The intention is to try to increase the stock of rental accommodation in the country, which is perilously low at this time, running at less than two per cent vacancy across the country and below one per cent in many major urban centres. We want to increase the rental accommodation stock for all Canadians in order, if at all possible, to avoid increasing rents.
The hon. member referred to the inefficient use of funds. Let me suggest that this is a most efficient use of funds. I think it is important that hon. members appreciate the difference between this legislation, which is to use the private sector funding, as opposed to limited dividend funding, which we intend to continue because it has been successful in the past. This is a most efficient use of funds, because with subsidies in the range of $16 million we expect to attract somewhere in the range of $1 billion into the mortgage market for low rental accommodation. In fairness, I should say that the $18 million to attract $1 billion is divided between home ownership and limited dividend rental accommodation.

March 25, 1975
National Housing Act
This seems to the government to be the most efficient way of using the taxpayers' money to get the greatest leverage possible. One should understand that we are dealing with private sector funds, to encourage building in that part of the market where there is an acute shortage and a need to get starts going on rental accommodation for the lower income group as quickly as possible. If one understands that, I think he can understand the balance of the argument.
As hon. members know, when I first assumed this portfolio last fall we experimented with a $50 million limited dividend rental program. We found there was an enormous response. As a result of discussions and studies we are now confident that there is a substantial amount of private funds that could find its way into the rental market, but only for higher income groups. This would not produce rental accommodation which the average Canadian can afford.
The intention here, therefore, is to apply the subsidies so as to encourage rental agreements with the owners who will accept those in lower income groups at lower rents. If the owner does not do that he does not qualify. This will be monitored by CMHC officers across the country so that we know the benefits are passed on to the tenants. If within five years the tenants' incomes increase, as they have continued to increase in Canada, we see little purpose in using taxpayers' money to subsidize their rents. In the meantime, we are increasing the stock of rental accommodation in Canada, which is important in trying to reduce the pressure on rents across the board.
The hon. member suggested that the owner could then sell out. If the hon. member will read clause 5(2)(b) he will see that the project or any part thereof shall not be sold or otherwise disposed of during the term of the agreement, except with the consent of the corporation and on terms and conditions approved by the corporation. By stating it this way we are discouraging those who are in the construction business building apartments from building these for low income people, but we can help that by subsidizing, and we hope that as their incomes increase, as they have constantly under Liberal governments, they will be in a better position to afford higher rents. In the meantime, they are being assisted and the landlord is bound to pass on that assistance.
The hon. member also refers to building standards. I think there is some confusion between building standards and maintenance standards. The building standards will be those of CMHC with regular inspections to make sure that standards are at a level of high quality and safety. In respect of maintenance standards, we require that they maintain adequate standards. The amendment would impose sort of a control over maintenance. Maintenance has not been found to be a major problem in the past as municipalities frequently monitor this aspect. We monitor it through the corporation, and certainly the tenants monitor it. We think it would be a built-in disincentive to provide a large volume of rental accommodation for low income groups whom this legislation is designed to attract.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say I am puzzled by most of the things the minister

said. Let me begin by reminding members of the House that, despite all the minister's glowing predictions and assumptions, the fact is that every month since the minister took office the housing picture in Canada has become worse. When we were debating this bill several months ago, the minister was still talking about his target of 210,000 housing units to be built in 1975. Since that time, we have the official figures released, not by critics of the government, not by members of the opposition parties and not by organizations such as the Canadian Council for Social Development, but by the minister's department.
Here is a news release issued on March 10 by CMHC- with which the minister seems to have some slight connection although I sometimes wonder if there is any at all- entitled "Preliminary February Housing Starts" and marked "for immediate release". It reads:
Housing starts during February were at a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 156,600 for all areas, according to preliminary figures released today by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Actual starts during the month in the urban areas were 5,031, a decline of 44 per cent from the 9,029 recorded for the same month one year ago.
Starts of single detached dwellings during the month totalled 2,177, a decline of 48 per cent from February, 1974. Starts of multiple dwellings declined 41 per cent to 2,854.
So, while the minister is telling us that his objective is to have 210,000 units built and that his programs will accomplish this, in fact what we see is a startling and continuing decline in the number of housing units being built.
More than that, when you look at what the government is prepared to do, you see that the amount of money which the minister and the government propose for capital expenditures, and which they propose to give to CMHC, is increased for 1975 over 1974 by just 12V4 per cent. That is just the amount of the increase in inflation this past year, and it is less than the increase in government expenditures for the coming fiscal year as compared with last year. The increase in government expenditures is 15 per cent, but the minister proposes to allocate only another 12 lA per cent to CMHC. So, in fact, we will get less housing units than we did last year.
The minister says that, of course, the government is giving a subsidy of $18 million to builders and that will bring in another $1 billion into the housing industry. That, according to my arithmetic, is a subsidy of 1.8 per cent. Surely, the minister is not telling us that the housing industry, the land developers, the servicing of land, the actual building of houses and of rental units have been operating on such a small margin that $18 million, a subsidy of 1.8 per cent, will suddenly bring into the market $1 billion. The fact is the figures demonstrate that builders are not building individual homes, they are not building condominiums or apartment units, because the cost of a mortgage is such that there is not the demand which is required.
More than that, the minister is following a deliberate policy. The minister and the government have made a political decision. Perhaps in terms of where the votes are, it is a very sound decision. People in Canada have bought the myth, the idea, that everybody should aim to own their own homes. Therefore, people with incomes of $5,000 up to $8,000, $10,000 or $12,000 believe, because we have such
March 25, 1975

ministers as the present minister telling them that it is possible for them to own their own homes, that that is possible. So the minister has deliberately taken more and more money, which in other years was allocated for use in the building of public housing units, to devote to programs such as the Assisted Home Ownership Program. I am not critical of the minister trying to meet the needs of people who qualify under that program because they need housing, but they are people who are not anywhere near the bottom of the economic ladder. They are people who have not been able to own their homes and who have rented their homes. The minister proposes to take money, which in other years was allocated to public housing or to senior citizens housing, and put it into programs such as AHOP and to subsidize limited dividend housing.
What is the result of that? I do not have the figures in front of me, but according to the information which I have been able to obtain, every province has already been told by the government and by CMHC that they will have less money for public housing this coming year than they had last year. I am told, for example, that the province of Ontario and metropolitan Toronto had planned to build 8,000 senior citizens' units and 2,000 fimily units in 197576. As I have already said, the minister has decided that the middle income groups need help more, so now apparently the province of Ontario and metropolitan Toronto will only get enough money from the government- because they are cutting back on public housing money, on the kind of money required to build senior citizens housing developments-to build 2,000 senior citizens units instead of the 8,000 units which they planned to build, and 500 family units instead of the 2,000 which they planned to build. That is the effect which the government's program is having.
Last year, according to the analyses which have been made, 24 per cent of the CMHC budget was aimed at low income groups. This year, because of the increased desire of the government for programs such as AHOP, instead of increasing the percentage of money available for housing for low income groups, the percentage will drop from 24 per cent, which I suggest was much too low, to 22 per cent. This is the kind of decision the minister and the government are making Mr. Speaker. It is not because the need is greatest for programs such as subsidizing limited dividend housing, but because the minister and the government believe that that is politically attractive. Private industry is not interested in public housing or in limited dividend housing. The only time it is interested in that kind of housing is in situations such as we have today when, no matter what they do, the prospective private home owner or purchaser simply is not there. Then, when the regular channels have dried up, when the cost of land is so high that the potential private purchaser cannot afford to buy a house, when the mortgage rate is so high that the prospective purchaser cannot afford to buy a house and when the building industry and the developers are in trouble because the so-called free enterprise system does not permit them to operate profitably, they are interested in building public housing units. Only then are they interested in building limited dividend housing.
National Housing Act
The minister has said that the government and CMHC will make sure that the housing units provided under this program will be up to standard. They have never done it up until now-and not just for limited dividend housing. How many ministers in charge of housing have promised legislation which would provide the purchaser of a home financed through Central Mortgage assistance with a warranty so that if he finds in a year or two that there are serious defects in the building he would have recourse? For how many years has that been promised by this minister and ministers before him? This minister said it was just a matter of a month or two, and now we find that there is nothing happening in regard to warranties. If a warranty cannot be provided to guarantee a purchaser under government programs that he is buying a house which is structurally sound, and which will not have major defects, how much more difficult will it be to provide guarantees on housing built by private builders? Private builders do not necessarily want to provide housing under government programs, but when they cannot get into other types of building, they make use of the fact that the minister is providing the money. What guarantees are there that CMHC and the government will do a better job than they have in the past on regular housing? And as my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) says, why five years? Why not ten years or fifteen years or longer?
Governments in Germany and in Scandinavian countries are building housing units, and they are saying in advance that their housing units will remain in good shape for 100 years. The minister is saying that, because he cannot get the builders to build for people who cannot afford to pay the market price, we must build limited dividend housing and give subsidies. But the government does not give the subsidies to those people who cannot afford to pay the rent; the subsidies are given to the builders. Moreover, the government does not require the builder to guarantee his work for a period of more than five years. Surely, we have our priorities backwards. I do not suppose we will ever have enough money to put into housing, but surely whatever money there is should be spend for those people who need housing the most; that is, not for people who hope to be covered under AHOP, not for people who will be covered by limited dividend housing, but for people who need housing the most.
It could be a lot better and should be a lot better for people for whom we are supposed to have been providing housing under our various public housing programs. Surely, that is where the money should have been directed. Surely, the minister could have done that, but if he is going to put the money into limited dividend housing, which I and my colleagues think is a mistake, then he ought to ensure that the limited dividend housing which is built will be of a standard of which we will not have to be ashamed as we have up until now. The minister shakes his head. The fact is that a great deal of the limited housing developments built in the past under other ministers were clearly inadequate, and I am sure not planned to stand for 100 years. As the years go by, we can see as we walk or drive along our streets how inadequate those housing units are.

March 25, 1975
National Housing Act

Motion No. 2.
That Bill C-46, an act to amend the National Housing Act, be amended by deleting clause 5.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I tried with all my Irish persuasion to have members of the House accept the first motion which I thought was a reasonable one. It was not accepted, so this is a second attempt to appeal to the reason of hon. members on a very important point. I raised the point in the first motion. I want to delete the entire section which provides subsidies to private builders of rental housing, and I have set forth my reasons. Builders have had a heyday with regard to capital costs and allowances. We are now going to give them subsidies, but we are not going to have any control over construction and maintenance standards. After five years we are going to give them the opportunity to sell these units that they are renting to tenants and they are going to make a capital gain. This is a
March 25, 1975

very inefficient use of the capital available for housing. The government has added insult to injury by passing the mortgage insurance on to the private companies rather than retaining it in the control of CMHC.
Those were the main arguments I used on the first motion, and they are the main arguments I put forward on the second motion. I repeat, we have a problem in Canada with regard to housing. I am glad the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) is here because he is a man of intelligence and compassion and I want to direct my remarks to him.
We have a critical housing situation in Canada. The situation as outlined by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) shows that it is the people in the lower income groups who are affected. The Postmaster General is concerned about these people and we in the New Democratic Party say that the moneys of CMHC as well as private money should be directed to taking care of those people.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs has said that over 800,000 people pay more than 25 per cent of their income for rent. He said that 107,000 people who earn less than $3,000 a year pay 50 per cent of their income for rent. We say that these moneys should be directed to two sectors-the public housing sector and the non-profit co-op sector. Is anything more reasonable than that?
May I point out what the minister has done, Mr. Speaker? In December he issued a statement to CMHC setting forth that the federal rental housing program had produced 18 projects for family housing. At that time he attempted to use CMHC money to build housing units for family rental, more especially for the lower income groups. I am sure the Postmaster General will be concerned, because he is concerned about low income people in Toronto.
This is what the Minister of State for Urban Affairs did, Mr. Speaker. He had Green Glen Developments build an apartment complex at the northeast corner of Jane and Finch streets in Toronto and gave CMHC $12,278,000 to build 229 one bedroom units, 66 two bedroom units and 132 three bedroom units. He wants to solve the problem of low income people by building a 33 story complex to house them. I am sure the Postmaster General knows how he would feel if he were one of the people living in that 33 storey building with a family. I am sure he can fully appreciate the social problems that will flow from that type of development.
This approach to rental housing only creates social problems and should not be permitted. Loans to the builders are given at 8 per cent for 15 years. If the minister wants to build homes for low income people, he should provide a low interest rate. If the minister wants $1 billion for housing, he can get it. He should say to private institutions like banks, insurance and trust companies, "You have a social responsibility to fulfil to those on low incomes and you should assign a certain percentage of your money to such people at low interest rates." That is what the minister ought to do. But does he do it? Not for a minute, Mr. Speaker. He goes to the builders and developers-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman had a lot of fun at the Postmaster General's expense, which is quite normal these days, almost as much fun as I had when considering the hon. member's dual policy on industrial relations, a dual policy made evident last evening when he and members of his party voted in favour of ordering striking longshoremen in British Columbia back to work. He and his colleagues were being pragmatic.
The minister is a man of compassion-I say this sincerely-and he is trying to be realistic in housing policies. Ideally, I suppose everyone in this country should live in a nice, self-contained bungalow, on a lot 50 by 100. Many of us bought homes like that after the end of the second world war, when land was reasonable. I myself bought one through Central Mortgage and Housing; even then the mortgage was not easy to pay.
Most of the present ministers' policies are aimed at helping low income families. He has tried to induce private funds into the market, in an effort to see that the private industry assumes its social obligations. I understand the hon. member's point about a 33-storey apartment building. But we must face reality; look at things as they are in the centre of Toronto. Land there is very expensive. I suppose the alternative to the hon. member's scheme is to say that because land is so expensive in the centre of Toronto, because it is so expensive to build anything in the heart of Toronto, poor people in the Toronto area must live 55 miles from the centre of the city.

Mr. Speaker, let me say to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) that we hoped that, with the appointment of a new minister in charge of housing, we should see a fundamental change from the sort of housing policy the government has followed for the past number of years. We hoped for a change in the direction of the Canadian housing policy, and we do not have it. We are witnessing more of the same. Let us not forget the point of the amendment, the point which the Postmaster General forgot to mention. It is this; we should quit subsidizing those who do not need subsidies. Instead, we should put more of the money we save into low income and limited dividend housing. That should stimulate housing starts in Canada and represent a change in policy. Such change in policy is long overdue.
The Postmaster General is concerned about basic human rights, about which the people in this country and members of the United Nations are also concerned. But is not a basic right the right to decent housing? Apparently that right is not extended to low income people. Under this government the developers have the right to charge all the market will bear and speculators and developers have the right to do their worst. You know, the money changers were driven from the temple 2,000 years ago but they "snuck" in through the back door under this government's housing policies.
A fundamental change is necessary with regard to how we are going to develop housing for low and middle income families sufficient to meet their needs. This will not be accomplished by following the same method we have been using since the end of World War II. It is not going to happen. By following the concept of charging all that the traffic will bear and allowing usurious interest rates to be levied against people with low and middle incomes, we will not succeed. The subsidies now being provided for the industry, the builders, developers and land speculators, should be used to subsidize interest rates for low and middle income families. Those earning less than $8,000, $9,000 or $10,000 a year should get an interest rate on their mortgages of 6 per cent. They would then get their houses built. They would either build them themselves or hire developers to build them.
There should be a freeze on land prices in our cities and the suburbs. We should quit allowing land to change hands two or three times through interlocking companies with a markup each time. We should put an end to the uncivilized and inhuman situation of allowing a 50 by 100 foot lot to sell for $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 or $30,000. That is not free enterprise. That even flies in the face of the principles and concepts of members opposite, but yet they perpetuate policies and legislation that continues along the same line. That is why we are trying to put forward these amendments.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) knows the situation for low and middle income earners. He has worked with those people. In fact, he lived in those circumstances. The red herrings that the minister dragged into his remarks do not help. As one of the leaders in cabinet, I thought he would try to persuade the minister responsible for housing and his other colleagues to make the fundamental change in housing policy that is required so that
