speechtext:
that Bill C-230, to amend the Criminal Code (obscene broadcasting), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to bring broadcasters, referring specifically to CBC television, within the Criminal Code provisions respecting offences that tend to corrupt morals. This simply means that the general public would be provided with an avenue through which such person or persons could be charged with a criminal offence. There is no intent here to define what is obscene, immoral or indecent-that is the responsibility of the code of law.
At present there is no vehicle available to the Canadian taxpayer to effectively control CBC programs for which they are forced to pay an increasing amount each year. They can only express their opinions to members of parliament or to the CBC but, due to the protection that Crown corporations enjoy through lack of government interference, and under the cloak of the Canadian Radio-Television Commission, their complaints prove to be an exercise in futility. If the CRTC would follow a set of guidelines established by the majority of Canadians, and if the CBC
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Penner).]
could be held responsible for its actions, this type of legislation would not be necessary.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is aimed at the CBC, the expenses of which could be construed as a levy of $15 on every man, woman and child in Canada, or an expenditure of over $350 million this year. When people pay for a product, they have the right to a product they can appreciate and enjoy. Unfortunately, in the minds of taxpayers, during the past five to seven years there has been rapid and continuing depreciation in the value of the CBC. In this age of technology, knowledge should be increasing and improving-there are greater opportunities to learn. Why then should we have vulgar and corrupt programs inflicted upon viewers by this publicly-funded outlet? I cannot accept the two-bit statement of those who ask if there is not a switch on a TV set or, if CBC productions are so objectionable, why is it requested to extend into new areas. Anyone who makes this type of remark is missing the point entirely, as is the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) who merely says he will relay the complaints of MPs to the CBC.
If criticism had any effect at all on the CBC, we would not be required to bring up such matters in this House. Why should anyone in this country have to turn off his TV because of a despicable CBC program for which he is paying? As long as the CBC is a Crown corporation, operated by public funds, it has a responsibility, as does the government, to provide satisfactory programs for residents in every area of our country. If the CBC will not furnish acceptable services out of the millions of dollars it spends, why not sell it to permit a private firm to provide enjoyable entertainment? At least then taxpayers' dollars would not be involved.
Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary for me to take time to give more details to this House, because members of parliament are well aware of the dissatisfaction of constituents, and in some cases of their anger, about CBC shows. Time does not permit me to list the numerous objectionable productions emanating from that corporation, but I do want to focus attention on one in particular-The Ten Lost Years-which was apparently an attempt to depict the hard years of the thirties. While those were difficult years, they were not lost years for those who struggled through them. "Lost" could better be applied to those whose thinking is so badly warped they could not portray what did happen during the depression due to inability to comprehend; instead, they foisted their interpretation of life today on those earlier years.
I would like to read, now, a letter which was addressed to the CBC, a copy of which I received:
Sunday evening productions under the guise of 'Canadiana' (not to be confused with either drama or entertainment) are consistently so bad that I, for one, am asking the Minister of Communications and Transport, and also my local member of parliament to get you off the air. 'Ten Lost Years', your effort of last evening, indicated clearly the group of alleged performers lack both direction and talent; even the minor character parts were terrible.
Mr. Speaker, the most unfortunate aspect of that entire program, other than its vulgarity, was neglect in not portraying the down-to-earth philosophy of our countrymen who brought Canada through those troubled times. The depression of the 'thirties was world-wide; it was not unique to us in Canada, and we have to accept that fact,
March 25, 1975

but added to the woes of western Canadians was the drought which hit the prairies. The only drought revealed in the "Ten Lost Years" was the dearth of facts, and the drought in the minds of its producers.
The producers used the setting of the hard times of the 'thirties to place emphasis on the standards of a sick segment of our society. I want to quote from a letter which reads:
Today a percentage of our society has a tendency to render the minimum of service for the greatest possible gain. Thoughts of making a contribution are completely lacking, and to say this unfortunate philosophy extends throughout the world of today, or that it is worse in other countries, is really a poor excuse for having it obtained in Canada.
Canadians who lived through the drought and the depression of the thirties did not ask for, expect or receive government handouts which are ordinary procedure today. They faced the difficulties of those years with fortitude and determination; defeat was not part of their make-up.
"Ten Lost Years" did not depict the shipping of carloads of vegetables donated by residents outside the drought area to the needy; it did not depict farmers removing their remaining physical resources in covered wagons several hundred miles to a new land, without complaint, to start again; it did not depict the endless hours of toil, all to no avail because tractors were sitting idle in sheds or fields without fuel to operate. Horsepower had to be relied upon to till the soil. The program did not show the farmers who managed to feed their stock using horses to build roads to work out their taxes; it did not show women, urban and rural, taking picnic baskets to community picnics without cost to anyone to enjoy ball games and other sports at a time when such tremendous value was placed on fellowship. The show did not depict Saturday nights when those fortunate enough to possess radios waited with anticipation to welcome neighbours to hear musical programs of fun, of class and moral fibre; it did not portray crops being blown out by the roots and fences completely buried by topsoil, powder-dry for lack of moisture. No mention was made of the fact that the Canadian Wheat Board came into its own in those years, or that the Bank of Canada was founded for the benefit of Canadians. No, the creators of this falsification did not do so because, even with their expertise at degrading, which was their obvious goal, they could not penetrate either corporation.
Mr. Speaker, the CBC sacrificed a wonderful opportunity to provide entertainment of educational worth and vivid recollection and, either due to lack of initiative or disregard for reality, chose to place emphasis through calculated deception on immorality and obscenity in a complete distortion of the truth. Canadians who know, through experience or otherwise, what actually did happen in the 'thirties are not willing to have their tax dollars spent on programs neither suitable for viewing nor factual. This bill, if passed, could be the basis of control over productions which exceed approved limitations. I trust my proposal will receive the support of all good parliamentarians.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am quite moved by the warm welcome I am receiving. I am pleased to say a few words on Bill C-230 introduced by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) who has just stated why he introduced this bill.
Its purpose is to amend the Criminal Code to make it perhaps even more illegal than it is already to broadcast obscene representations and matters. I would like first of all to congratulate the hon. member for his courage in introducing such an imaginative bill in this House. I appreciate that he certainly represents the views of the voters in his riding. Having recently sat on the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, I know for a act that several members are concerned about having received mail from their voters about dramatic programs that were shown on the national network, and particularly the English network of the CBC.
I know the hon. member certainly received mail from his constituents, and as their view corresponds no doubt to his, he moved in the direction he did today, and I can only commend him for that. However, I am not sure myself I share the same views. The hon. member's purpose is commendable in that it states in this House what seems to be a regional concern. On the other hand, the bill he introduced, if passed, would have a national bearing, and that bothers me somewhat. I also represent people from downtown Montreal, people who never miss an opportunity to let me know, as their member of Parliament and chairman of the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts of the House of Commons, when they are not satisfied with programs they see on the national network and the private networks.
However, in the case of programs referred to, namely "Ten Lost Years" or other programs recently mentioned at the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts such as "Baptizing" and other programs whose names I forgot, I did not receive any adverse comment from my constituents. I do not think there was much either in Ontario. It was at both ends of the country, more especially in rural areas of Canada, that those programs disturbed the people.
Now, I already see a weakness. The member is concerned by an apparently regional problem. I do not think that hon. members-after all, they do represent the entire country-will blindly pass such a bill.
For the information of some members who did not have the opportunity to attend the last sittings of the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, I repeat some views put forward by the CBC authorities on the lewdness or alleged lewdness of some programs. For instance, Mr. Picard said that it is difficult, in this day and age, if the corporation truly wants to discharge its mandate and depict our Canadian society as it is today, to picture only the bright side of things because, unfortunately, our society also has its dark side.
What is news? As always, more often than otherwise, violence if not obscenity. But some would have the corporation overlook, in its productions, that aspect of Canadi-

March 25, 1975
Criminal Code
an society; still, it is very real; that was one of the points Mr. Picard made.
He made another with regard to the artistic value of some plays broadcast, on request, by the corporation. Some of those plays have undeniable intrinsic value; still, it happens that in the course of the performance sex or violence are displayed.
In my opinion, if the play as a whole is not only an excuse for sex and violence, but tells a story which is logical, which makes sense, and which has an artistic value, I do not see why it should be rejected outright simply because there is a scene here and there of sex, for sex is an integral part of our lives. This does not mean that productions must be filled with sex, but I feel that we should not fall head over heels because we see a breast on the television screen, for these are quite normal things.
Do we want our state-run broadcasting system to waste its time depicting a Victorian style society which no longer exists, which falsely tries to show us a society which is made up of angels and which has nothing in common with reality? We do not expect that from our national broadcasting system, and we do not want it to become something like Moliere's Tartuffe,, if you know what I mean.
There is a question I wish to ask all hon. members. Should we censor the media? As a matter of principle, I feel that it is important to stop there. Films are no longer censored in the province of Quebec. Once they have been screened, they are either accepted or rejected in their entirety. Films no longer get clipped as they used to be. A decision is taken as to whether the film is acceptable or not. Those which are deemed acceptable certainly contain scenes which some people can normally be expected to find offensive. Otherwise, if you do not want to offend anyone, you will not show anything daring, and you will probably end up displeasing those who would like to see daring scenes. You cannot make everybody happy. And yet, a middle-of-the-road policy is certainly not impossible bearing in mind that viewers always can exercise a control over what reaches their households through electronic media. The listener who doesn't like a program has ample freedom to turn off his set, watch another program, read his paper or even do at home what he does not like to watch on TV.
I wonder if we should censor media and run the risk of hindering creativity. In all media there are devoted people whose work it is to show people what comes out of their creative minds, to show things with an artistic value. Frequently, the shows which are programmed are based for instance on books, on novels. For example, everybody heard about a film entitled The Carpet Baggers, of course a very bold one. Yet the film was based on a novel which was a best-seller. If everybody rushes to buy that book, how could a film producer be smitten with remorse and regret or ask himself a million questions before he starts shooting his film?
Media may be censored if the matter arises, but whoever does so should wonder what the results may be from a creative point of view. It can be done, but only after it has been thought over.

Do we want to run the risk of describing an artificial society, I shall refer to it presently, a holy society that does not exist? All kinds of directions can be given to our media. Parliament can even force them, if it so wishes, to show nice things only. We know that in other countries, national television corporations used to show the people nothing but nice things; but of course those nations came to require more freedom, and certainly the intention here is not to restrict the freedom of the media.
Finally, the basic question arises; Are we to take the decisions for the people? The decision to watch or not to watch TV, to turn the radio on or not to do it is a personal decision, a matter of choice very easily exercised by the people. They can be deprived of that choice, but we should first ask listeners and the general public whether such is their wish. I do not believe that such a decision can be taken in the course of this kind of one-hour debate. I am not inferring the decision would be intrinsically bad, if a majority of Canadians were to tell us: Choose what we are going to see. Maybe that decision will be made in the future. But before acting, we should await the order to do so.
I would emphasize at this point that the Criminal Code, contrary to what the hon. member for Red Deer apparently feels, already includes a number of provisions on obscenity. Criminal charges may already be laid in cases of obscene showings on television. Through this bill, the member seeks more specific measures. This is of some concern to me, because creativity could be restricted in the process. Television and radio producers already live under some sort of threat. In addition to the Criminal Code, the Canadian Radio-Television Commission has coercive powers much more effective than amendments to the Criminal Code. The CRTC already established regulations on obscenity, and they can even suspend media licences. That is much more serious than putting an employee of the medium in prison for a month. This sword of Damocles is much more likely to make owners of media think twice than the proposed amendment to the Criminal Code.
Since provisions to that effect already exist in the code, I wonder if the bill is not more an answer to a purely

Madam Speaker, I was listening to the translation and not directly at this distance to the hon. members' remarks but certainly the word "rural" was used, as well as the suggestion that the whole thing was a regional matter. I have received a fair amount of mail in the last three weeks on this issue from points all the way from Truro, Nova Scotia, to Vancouver Island, and a fair portion of it came from the province of Ontario and from the urban metropolis of Toronto. I would suggest that almost all the voices from across that space, from the larger centres as well as the smaller, were saying the same thing to me. I do not accept the idea that the problem is appreciated only by a few people in one particular area of the country.
The problem is nationwide and undoubtedly worldwide. When we read publications from other lands we see that it is not isolated to Canada, in any way, shape or form. The putdowns come in a variety of ways. During a session of the committee I referred to a letter written by John Hirsch, head of t.v. drama, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Toronto. He sent the letter out to the major newspapers of this country. In this regard there was some particular discussion of programming, and Mr. Hirsch said in his letter:
It is a matter of determining the role of the CBC in the consideration and formation of public taste; that is, whether the corporation is to follow or to lead in such matters.
Obviously it is not up to CBC to go wildly off into avant-garde styles and far-out situations and language, but rather to remain just a few steps ahead of the whole viewing public in such matters.
Criminal Code
If one looks at the whole picture there seems to be a sort of downward slide rather than a process of elevating or raising the level of the standard of value. When there seems to be a downward slide one is suspicious of any writer that talks about being ahead of the general public in a direction in which one would not wish to see the country or its broadcasting moving. Certainly, if one watched the television production "You'll Be All Right, Jamie Boy" he will know that this was pretty far out both in circumstance and language, and deserving of a fair amount of criticism.
Mr. Hirsch then went on to describe recent years' programming and he described it as a diet of harmless, rather blah material from CBC drama of little significance, programs that were made to be turned off, and he said the vigour and challenge came from American programs. I am not questioning the accuracy of what he describes about CBC programming over recent years, but it seems to me that the answer to that problem is not to go from bad to worse but to make some effort to improve the situation. In talking about American programming Mr. Hirsch says that they have managed to handle such difficult subjects as abortion, homosexuality, gang-rape, wife swapping and other purported untouchables.
One thing that concerns me very much about all of this is the attempt to build an unshockable viewing audience. I would be very much concerned about a nation whose national network, or any network, handled some of the subjects in the list given to us by Mr. Hirsch and it produced no critical response to and through members of parliament. That would concern me, because I think that by that time we would be sunk in apathy a long way, and we would be at a point where we would not react any more to situations that should give us cause to react. I have been concerned about this for a long time.
When I am not in parliament, I teach school. A year ago, browsing along a bookshelf I picked up a book called "Go Ask Alice". I am surprised that it has not made the roster of CBC drama programs. It purports to be the diary of a 14 or 15 year old girl who is a drug addict. It is truly the bottom. The class I had at school used to write tiny book reviews for me and I always told them to write about anything they had read, it did not matter where they read it. I discovered over the course of a few weeks that several people in my class had read "Go Ask Alice" and spoke of it in most glowing terms.
When I asked one day in class how many people had read the book, about five girls put up their hands. I asked then how many of them thought it was a good book, and all five hands went up again. It concerned me that they should see that particular book as a good book. It was truly the bottom in terms of language, in terms of lack of a plot, and in terms of ripping off young people by purporting to be on the level of "The Diary of Anne Frank". The cover purported the books to be similar. So I asked my pupils why they thought it was a good book, and they said to me, "That is the way it is, that is where it's at."
Again I am concerned about the acceptance of an utter lack of standards, the absence of everything one might call traditional morality. I was very concerned about Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
Criminal Code
Hirsch's defence of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in his letter when he said:
Now the Canadian viewer suddenly finds himself confronted on our drama programs with an image that is his own. He sees that he is like others.
I would hope that the Canadian viewer was not confronting himself on some of the recent programming on CBC. I would hope we were not at that level yet. I would hope there were still some happy families in this country, some fathers who were respected by their children and beloved by their wives, that there were within the country some normal family relationships because, if there are not, then we are in a bad way indeed.
Finally Mr. Hirsch said:
In other words, we have to give the viewers not only what they think they want, we have to give them the kind of high quality that the honest, creative artists we are trying to employ know they will want once they try it, and once they get to like it.
I was extremely concerned about the analogy to feeding a small child a variety of vegetables that he does not want to eat but that he should eat. Very often, children are exposed to those vegetables gradually to get used to the taste and eventually find themselves liking it. The argument there is usually that the offending food is nutritious and of value. But I would be very suspicious of the same effort going into conditioning the Canadian public to some of the recent programming that they have had on the CBC. I would be concerned indeed if a public shown "You'll be all right, Jamie Boy" would not be shocked by it, and would not resent in particular the point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer that they were paying for it at the same time.
I do not wish to limit my remarks to the CBC because there is a great deal we should consider seriously about the whole spectrum of television broadcasting in this land. I am one who believes in the abolition of the death penalty, and yet as I watch television occasionally-one does not have to watch it very closely, all you have to be is in the next room listening to the sound effects-I recognize the compendium of crime, violence, torture and rape that is placed before the Canadian public night after night, usually starting early in the day and placed before small children and often babies. Given that it is not much wonder if we seem to be retreating into violence and retreating from our standards and abandoning moral values. That is one thing of which we should be very careful.
There are other programs that would almost qualify for the label of obscene. Here again one moves into matters of opinion, but when you see a "Miss Teenage Canada Pageant," for example, one sees a sort of exploitation of those people. That was not a CBC but a CTV program. I think one wonders about the value and the contribution that will be made to this country by that sort of program.
I am also concerned that those people who question such programs become the recipients of the kind of criticism that was directed at the members of the broadcasting committee in this morning's issue of the Globe and Mail by columnist Geoffrey Stevens. What one says is characterized as a "knee-jerk reaction," and the entire committee is labelled as grossly incompetent and having spent its time on programming rather than on any diligent seeking out

of the financing that goes behind the CBC. I do not see much point in digging too deeply into the CBC financing if the question in the minds of the public concerns the product that comes out at the end. That is one of the areas at which we can and should look.
I hope that voices in the House will continue to hold to their critical faculty and not be afraid to express it, because I still feel that across this land there is a great majority who want something better and expect something better from television.
One of the things which worries me about our Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is that I suspect the young writers of Canada, or the honest creative artists of this country, while they may be very honest and very creative, quickly learn what can be sold to the organization and begin to tailor their product accordingly. I think the same is somewhat true of films. One would hope that we could still find a market for a dramatic presentation of a family which triumphs rather than of a family which always fails.
The previous speaker mentioned the CRTC, and it seems to me that as the years have gone by, with the change of name and the change of function, that body has in a sense lost some of the authority and the concern it had when it was known as the Board of Governors of the CBC. In that older name there was the suggestion of some watching over, and some guiding along the lines which are hoped for in the bill presented this afternoon. I am afraid that that control and that concern are now rather lost.
I can appreciate the despair in the letters which come to me from people who feel they are voiceless. They know that something is wrong, and they sense this very deeply. Yet they cannot make any impact at all. They then turn to their member of parliament and hope that a voice will be raised somewhere. I trust that these voices will not be silenced by the kind of criticism which has been handed out to members of the broadcasting committee over these last few days because they have dared to raise questions of real concern to a great many people in this country.
I feel that there is room for the CRTC to be some kind of watchdog. I realize that there are avenues which could be followed at the present time by someone objecting to programming in terms of launching a suit, but I realize as well that for the average citizen, whether he lives in a great city or in a rural area, the problems of effectively launching a suit against the CBC, or against the CRTC, are very great indeed and are not likely to be undertaken.
I do trust that as a result of the debate we have been having in the last three weeks, and as a result of all the letters which have been written, we can have a good look at the kind of programming which is too prevalent and be prepared to do something, not just about what is usually called obscenity or bad language, but particularly about the violence, the bloodshed, the treatment of law enforcement officers-those factors which must play a role in the rising tide of crime facing this country.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING OFFENCES THAT TEND TO CORRUPT MORALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), and the concern of many hon. members in
March 25, 1975

this House and of people across the country about the programs which appear not only on our national network but on all networks, and in all facets of the communications industry. They are concerned, whether they are from rural areas or urban areas, about the use of obscenity, profanity and immoral activities by anyone, whether it be in broadcasting, newspapers, or books. No matter where it may be, I feel that close scrutiny of such questionable material must be carried out at all times by those responsible for the activities of all broadcasters, reporters, advertisers, and all those related to the dissemination of information and entertainment, not only on the public broadcasting service, which seems to be the prime thrust of the concern here this evening, but on the private sector of broadcasting as well.
I am concerned that much of the criticism has been directed, whether rightly or wrongly, against the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and members of that broadcasting group. This bill states that everyone commits an offence who, being a broadcaster, or an officer of an employer of a broadcaster, allows to be broadcast an immoral, indecent or obscene performance, entertainment or representation. That takes in the complete segment of broadcasters, from those behind the microphones to the cameramen, script men, writers, producers and directors, no matter where they are in that broadcast segment. I think that perhaps in this respect we must consider where the broadcaster fits in, what he has done, and what regulations he is now concerned with regarding this matter.
Other hon. members will no doubt deal with the legal aspect of this bill, but in the next few minutes I would like to direct the attention of the House to the effect the bill will have on the broadcasters at the grass roots level of broadcasting. I believe that one of the first concerns would be a precise definition of what is obscene or immoral. As we have learned in the recent hearings of the broadcasting committee, of which I am a member-and I agree with much of what the previous speaker has said regarding reports of the broadcasting committee which have appeared in the newspapers recently-there is certainly a wide divergence of opinion even amongst the members, broadcasters and all the segments of our population as to what is immoral or indecent. What I may feel is immoral or indecent other members of this House may not feel is immoral or indecent, and I think that one of the first things we have to define is the common standard of immorality or indecency. It would be terribly difficult, if not impossible at this time, to arrive at that precise definition.
Last fall, for example, all of the networks presented scenes of the slaughter of calves performed publicly, scenes which immediately shocked a response from the general public and from this House as to the problems faced by the members of the agricultural community, and it was a response that was rightfully made at that time. Surely some segments or individuals in our society found those scenes to be distasteful. Some of them have told me that they found them to be very distasteful, but those are scenes which the farmer takes for granted because he sees them every day of the week in slaughter houses and in other situations. If this bill became law the private citizen could say that that was obscene and immoral, and bring a charge under the Criminal Code.
The Royal Assent
The bill before us now makes no comment with regard to the extreme violence that is seen not only in the public sector of broadcasting but in the private sector as well, and in many cases more so in the private sector. I believe the extreme violence depicted on television is of parallel importance to the matters raised by the hon. member for Red Deer with respect to immorality.
Another matter of great importance is the effect this bill would have on the level of broadcasting. The bill refers to "Every one... who, being a broadcaster-" That includes the disc jockey on morning radio, the cameraman, and even those members of the press gallery who are broadcasters. The provisions of this section of the Criminal Code would cover the situation where anything they said was considered obscene. Producers, directors, and even copywriters would be included.
This is a complex business which is regulated not only by the Canadian Radio and Television Corporation but by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. This association has a code of ethics which member stations follow, and it exercises control every step along the way. As well as being subject to the scrutiny of their profession members are, of course, subject to the provisions of the Criminal Code and the regulations of the CRTC.
At the present time the CRTC has authority to refuse to grant or renew licences in the broadcasting industry. It can also levy fines against a station or an individual broadcaster guilty of obscene, indecent or profane language or pictorial representation. The CRTC takes into consideration at the time of licence renewal any complaints that have been received from the general public about obscene programming. To my knowledge only a few fines have been levied in this respect and I believe they were against the private sector. I do not know of any renewal of licence having been refused by the CRTC on these grounds. I should draw to the attention of the House the self-regulatory-Mr. Speaker, I note the arrival of Black Rod.

speechtext:
motion No. 3:
That Bill C-46, An Act to amend the National Housing Act, be amended in Clause 6 by striking out lines 28 to 38 at page 3 and by substituting the following therefor:
"(2) Subsection 15.1(3) of the said Act is repealed.".
He said: Madam Speaker, the amendment I am moving at this time is very important. The two amendments I moved this afternoon were not very well received by the minister and the Liberal party and, I am sorry to say, the members of the Conservative party.
The substance of the first two amendments was directed at the private sector. We in the New Democratic Party are opposed to giving subsidies to builders and developers. Motion No. 3 is an opportunity for the members of the Liberal party, especially the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), to redeem themselves and to vote for a particular sector of the housing industry. I refer specifically to the non-profit sector.
The non-profit sector has had a rather short but impressive history with regard to housing in Canada. The reason is because it has embraced a large number of dedicated people who are prepared to work for little or no pay in order to solve the housing problem. They give some assistance to people with low and moderate incomes.
From time to time the government has been kind to the non-profit sector. I remind hon. members that under the present law the non-profit sector, which includes co-ops, was entitled to 100 per cent financing, a $10,000 start-up fund for its projects, and a 10 per cent capital grant. These appeared to be generous provisions, and they were. The

members of the non-profit sector appreciated that help from the government.
Originally they did not have that type of help. At the most they had 95 per cent financing. The government saw the need of the non-profit sector and its contribution to lowering housing prices. It gave those provisions and that help to that sector. As a result the government has experienced a great number of dedicated people trying to solve the problem, especially in the large urban areas. But those people experienced rising land costs which made it very difficult for them to operate. The government realized that, and the minister said he would try to make a change. He said he appreciated the high cost of land and the government would step in to allocate moneys so that land could be purchased by CMHC and leased to the non-profit sector.
In his announcement, the minister set forth the objective of CMHC to give further assistance to the non-profit sector by purchasing land and leasing it to that sector. However, when he made his statement he was very ambiguous as to what he was going to do. He, in effect, said that if the government applies moneys to purchase the land, it could not continue some of the other assistance.
I will remind hon. members of those provisions. There was the $10,000 start-up fund, 100 per cent financing, and the 10 per cent capital grant. He said, in a very ambiguous way, that if the government was going to give moneys to purchase lands, and the land is to be leased to them by CMHC, he was going to cut off their 10 per cent capital grant. This was the "either or" proposition that the minister put to the non-profit sector. This is the reason I am moving this amendment.
We had before us in committee a group of dedicated people representing different housing groups across the country, especially the city of Toronto. Their argument was all-persuasive. In fact I never heard so many compliments paid by members of the housing committee to the presentation that was given by the Toronto Non-Profit Housing Federation. I say again that these are young people who have dedicated their time, ability and energy to help solve the problem.
This group pointed out some of the great benefits of non-profit housing. They pointed out that the residents of non-profit and co-operative housing projects enjoy security of tenure, which is a vital ingredient in the healthy social environment that is necessary for both the individual and the community. In other words, there is security of tenure for the residents who occupy the rental units within a project.
They pointed out that the non-profit corporation manages the housing and allows for more control over the administration by the residents than does the private market rental. This means no huge government bureaucracy or tremendous overhead to manage housing, as in the case of public housing projects. They emphasised security of tenure and far more control over the administration. If Your Honour had been in the House this afternoon you would have heard some of the remarks by members of the NDP with regard to the administration of not only public housing projects but also limited dividend projects operated by the private sector.
March 25, 1975

Thirdly, they pointed out that the non-profit sector is aimed directly at providing accommodation for low and moderate income households. That is more than important, because of the attitude of the minister, and because the legislation favours the private sector and the middle income group rather than the low and moderate income groups.
They pointed out, fourthly, that non-profit housing is a non-inflationary form of housing, unlike other government housing programs. What they mean by that is that the acquisition of an existing unit for rental, or the building of a new project for the non-profit sector both have the object of not making a profit. If there is ever a philosophy that should be enunciated and implemented in regard to housing in Canada, it is the non-profit aspect.
If the profit aspect entered into education, for example, very few of us would ever have even a third or fourth grade education. If it entered into medicare, then we would not have the health care and assistance that we have today. These young people realize that if profit enters into housing and we want to implement the basic principle that people are entitled to decent housing at affordable cost, then we either have to make a profit out of housing itself, or operate on a minimum profit. This means that we do not increase the cost of land or buildings in this sector.
This is in direct contrast to the situation in the private sector, which treats housing as a commodity and tries to make as much money as it can in as short a time as possible. The result is the high land costs and high housing costs so prevalent across the country today. In the city of Toronto alone the average cost of a home is $54,000. With the high interest rates prevailing today it is very difficult for a person living in Toronto to buy a home.
The federation points out that if the minister did not continue the capital cost allowance provision and the subsidy, this would have a marked effect on the non-profit sector. To illustrate this it prepared a table which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister because I think it is of great importance. For a one bedroom apartment with a monthly rent of $216 in a non-profit project, a person would require an annual income of $10,400; with provincial assistance the income would have to be $9,200. This is a very high income for the average low income family to achieve.
In the case of a large family which requires a four bedroom apartment, the total monthly rent would be $416, and this would require an income of between $17,700 and $20,000. These two examples do not include the cost of the land. If you take $25,000 to be the average cost of land for a home in Toronto, you have to add at least $7,000 for the land cost.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) with regard to third sector housing on which I place a high value. This is a new and important initiative taken by my predecessor, and one which I am following with enthusiasm.
As the hon. member said, these projects are eligible for 100 per cent financing of the capital cost, 10 per cent forgiveness to compensate for the cost of land, and up to $10,000 in start-up fees for groups who build, buy, or manage low-cost housing. In addition provincial assistance is often available. If this is still not sufficient to bring rents down to a level tenants can afford, there are the new provisions of section 44(l)(b) of the National Housing Act which have just been applied to non-profit and co-operative housing units-this is a rent supplement whose cost is shared by the provinces and the federal government.
As the hon. member has stated, in some cases even a 10 per cent grant is not sufficient to cover the cost of land, especially in high rent areas such as Toronto. In situations of that sort we give non-profit groups an option; the CMHC will then buy the land and lease it back under an arrangement which will enable tenants to go in at rents low-income people can afford. So we are not proposing to take something away. On the contrary, this constitutes a significant benefit. These rents can be set at levels which low income people can afford. I hope these measures will encourage more non-profit groups to go forward in areas where land costs are unusually high.
The hon. member for Broadview is aware of my interest in this subject, and of the interest taken by members of my family in his constituency who are dedicated to this whole area of third sector housing. It is something in which I believe very deeply, bearing in mind the economic benefit to those involved, the enhancement of the community spirit which is bound to be present, the social benefits to those who are managing their own housing and, not least, the fact that these projects will eventually serve as a real countervailing force in the marketplace.
This is a movement to be encouraged. I encourage labour groups wherever I speak to them, as I did yesterday, to emulate the example of the United Auto Workers in moving into this area. Veterans groups will now be able to do so on a much greater scale as a result of the announcement made today by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). Legion branches, which are possessed of valuable property and the services of men who have been dedicated to this organization throughout their lives, will be able to take advantage of these provisions.
I do not know of any other nation in the world which has gone so far in doing something for yet another generation of veterans-not young veterans, as we were when we came back from the war, charging off to raise families in the country-we are a little more tired now, and those days cannot be recaptured-but more mature men and women whose needs are still to be served.
The provision which the hon. member for Broadview would remove is, I suggest, one of the most beneficial

which could be included in favour of low income and non-profit groups whose work I should like to see encouraged.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am puzzled by the comments the minister has made. I would be surprised if he could convince members of this group that he is right. After all, as I said earlier this afternoon, we sit in opposition and we have a different philosophy. What puzzles me is not that the minister cannot convince us, but that he cannot convince the few people, the far too few people, who have involved themselves in co-operative and non-profit housing. If one accepted the rousing comments the minister made a few moments ago one would think that co-operative housing is flourishing in this country, that hundreds of thousands of people are living in co-operative housing, and that an appreciable proportion of our housing needs is being met by co-operative housing. Nothing could be further from the truth. One half of one per cent of the housing accommodation in this country is made up of co-operative housing projects.
One of the largest projects in the country happens to be in Winnipeg, and most of the units are in my constituency. Not a year goes by but I hear complaints from the dozen or more people who spend hundreds of hours a year working to try to promote more co-operatives. They complain about how difficult it is to get anything from the minister, about the bureaucratic way in which the CMHC is conducted, about the time it takes between the initiation of a project and its completion. They say that by the time approval is finally obtained from the minister the people for whom the plan was intended no longer qualify and they have to move up to a higher income bracket.
As I say, what interests me is that the minister has not been able to convince the people who are really interested in co-operative housing that this legislation will really help. Looking through my files I see a report in the Globe and Mail of last August, according to which Mayor Crom-bie of Toronto, the people involved in the Labour Council, and the representatives of the non-profit housing organizations, are completely dissatisfied with the minister and his program.

I am not so concerned about the Mayor of Toronto. I know he is a Tory. But I am concerned about the people in the Labour Council and in the non-profit housing organizations in Toronto. They are saying that the minister's program and the legislation we are considering simply do not meet their needs.
Let me just refresh the minister's memory in case he has forgotten. The news report says:
The Labour Council of Metro Toronto's cooperative housing program has suffered the latest blow in a program that has endured several since the National Housing Act was amended in June, 1973, to permit 100 per cent mortgage financing for co-operative groups.
A week ago, Central Mortgage and Housing Corp. officials told the Labour Council that it could not use provincial subsidies to calculate the economic viability of its plan to build and rehabilitate 98 units-
March 25, 1975

And, they added, without the subsidies the projected rents were too high to consider financing the proposal.
That is precisely what the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) has said. The article then states:
The labour council has supported non-profit housing by community groups, and taken part in the acquisition of housing to be operated by the City of Toronto Non-Profit Housing Corp.
City politicians and officials, as well as people involved in non-profit housing groups, are afraid that if the Labour Council can't get CMHC approval for a non-profit proposal, with all the resources it has at its disposal, then no one can.
The Labour Council has said, as quoted in this article:
"Our hope of attracting community institutions to engage in housing will be seriously upset- "
These organizations have talked to the chairman of CMHC and to the minister, and have indicated that they are caught in the squeeze between rising costs in housing and the regulations set by CMHC. Mr. Teron sent a reply to these people and said:
"We do include any provincial subsidies in assessing the viability of projects.
Similarly, they do include the 100 per cent funding of land in the calculation, and it is this provision that has made it virtually impossible for co-operative housing organizations to expand. The minister is concerned about getting groups into housing, and he knows there has been a very marked drop in the number of housing starts this year. Here we have groups of people who are prepared to do a great deal of work. They are prepared to participate in the planning of the projects, of the units, and in respect of the acquisition and the best use of the land. These people are doing this work without pay, and are not as concerned as private builders with making profits.
In this day of high costs one would think the minister would be interested in helping these groups promote their ideas so that more people will get into co-operative housing. Instead the minister has said, as other ministers so frequently said in the past, that he is not really prepared to help co-operative housing groups in order that they can grow and build houses, setting guidelines in respect of housing so that the private sector cannot simply charge as much or more than the traffic will bear. This is the purpose of the amendment moved by my colleague. It is our hope that the government and parliament will do whatever is possible to encourage co-operative housing groups to become a meaningful factor in the provision of houses for Canadians.
Unfortunately the minister has simply not met any of the arguments put forward by these people, and it is obvious that he has no intention of doing so. We will hear more fine sentiment. As the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) suggests, the minister talks a good game, but when it comes to taking action or doing something for these groups of people who are prepared to do a job to meet some of the problems of housing, all we get from the minister is a flat no.
I must say I am disappointed with the minister. He made many excellent speeches in the early stages of his ministerial responsibility, and I really thought that for once, by choice or by accident, we had a minister who really cared about housing and about the needs of the ordinary and the poor people. To my regret I see that I was
National Housing Act
wrong, and that what we have is another minister who will agree that this is the right thing to do but will not bring in any legislation, or find the money, to do these things that are required.

speechtext:
motion No. 4:
That Bill C-46, an Act to amend the National Housing Act, be amended in Clause 8 by striking out line 22 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"in Council and in no case shall such rentals exceed 4 per cent of the book value to the Corporation of the land".
He said: Madam Speaker, this amendment applies directly to the non-profit sector. I thought we would have had some co-operation from the minister, members of the government party and members of the Conservative party in respect of assisting the non-profit sector to build more homes, but we did not get that co-operation.
The minister in his remarks referred to veterans housing and suggested what a great advantage this would be to veterans in conjunction with the announcement by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). Let me just take a few minutes to outline the purpose of this amendment.
The minister has said that if a non-profit group goes into a project in respect of which the land is purchased by CMHC the group is not entitled to the 10 per cent capital grant. We have tried to point out that if that is the case the rents that will have to be charged will be too high to shift the accommodation to the low and middle income groups. In addition, these groups should be given some idea as to what the rent is to be in respect of the land.
When a business acquires a building it sets up a schedule of depreciation for tax purposes that applies over the life of the building. I understand that if a brick building is involved it is set up for 40 years at 2V4 per cent. In these cases CMHC will be acquiring the land and there will be a 100 per cent factor to be set up in respect of the purchase of that land.

National Housing Act
Part of the non profit sector is saying through me that, if it has to purchase land, it should have some idea with regard to what it will cost over the life of the project, and the amendment says that it should not exceed 4 per cent over the life of the project. I would like the minister to get up and say that this is such a worthwhile program that we should charge them one dollar a year rent. This is a formula which the city of Toronto and other large cities use when they give land to non-profit groups. They say that in order to keep the rents down the cost of the land must be kept down. Being city property the cities give it to them for one dollar a year. I think the minister should do the same, but if he does not go along with the one dollar a year formula, CMHC regulations should not exceed 4 per cent of the cost of the land.
When we were in committee the minister said that he wanted to be more flexible and that he did not want to commit himself with regard to this matter. This means that CMHC regulations will give a discretionary power to the officials in CMHC, and they will indicate that a project really has to pay for itself, but they will not put in the cost of the land. We are saying that the minister and CMHC should indicate that in such worthy projects the rent should be one dollar a year. If that is not possible or feasible, then it should not exceed 4 per cent. If the non-profit project stops its function, then by charging one dollar a year rent there could be a provision in the lease whereby the land, and the building on the land, will revert to the ownership of CMHC. I ask the minister to help the non-profit sector. I have the feeling he wants to, but he is not doing it.
I have received the message from the non-profit sector that they are not the least bit pleased with the alternative method the minister has proposed because they know it will be a burden on their costs when they are trying to keep down rents for people in low income categories. It defeats the very purpose of the non-profit sector when it shifts from the low income group and only is available to the middle and upper income group. It puts the lower income group at the mercy of the only remaining sector with housing for them, and that is the public housing sector.
I hope that the minister will see the strength of this argument and, not only the strength of the 4 per cent, but really the strength of the one dollar per year rent with the provision that the land would revert to CMHC and, if the land reverts, the building thereon also reverts.

speechtext:
I appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Welland, and I hope he will take the opportunity to speak after I finish. I would like to tell the House that the percentage of the total housing stock in Canada under the wing of the non-profit sector is one half of one per cent, and the minister himself wants to increase that. We all want to increase it, and the only way we can increase it is by giving that sector help. The minister has restricted help. He has given the subsidies to the private builders, to the lending institutions like the banks and finance and trust companies, but what he has done to the non-profit sector is restrict its operation.
At the end of the year we will find that this sector's one half of one per cent of the total stock will be reduced even further. It will probably be one quarter of one per cent. This will not give us any pride; it will not give the Minister of State for Urban Affairs any pride, or the hon. member for Wellington. I think all of us should direct our attention and our energies to increasing the stock of nonprofit housing. We should encourage it.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has just turned around and looked at me, and I think he said, "John, you are right." I can just feel the vibrations from the hon. member for Hamilton West because he knows that in the city of Hamilton there are dedicated people in the non-profit sector who want to increase the number of units for low income people. I hope that at least he on the Conservative side will stand up and support it with all the strength he displays on other measures.
I hope that the minister will see the wisdom and the common sense of the amendment, agree with me, and undertake that the rents chargeable to the non-profit sector will either be one dollar a year with the reversion feature if the non-profit project ceases to operate or, at the very least, 4 per cent. If he did so, I am sure that the minister would be very proud.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I was invited to participate in this debate, and I am quite happy to do so.

speechtext: By whom?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was very impressed with the comments made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert). While I am not familiar with the quotations given a few moments ago from the Globe and Mail concerning the situation in Toronto and the problems there, I have learned over the years that land prices in Toronto are very high. One of the reasons housing has become almost impossible for even the middle income groups in this country is the high cost of land.
In my own area a number of organizations have been established over the years which built low rental units, and in most cases they have had to raise their rents, because of maintenance and other costs, to a point where
March 25, 1975

CMHC and the Ontario Housing Corporation have been invited back into them. I am thinking particularly of one which involves quite a number of veterans and which is one of the first projects of this nature the Legion undertook. I am certainly in agreement that one of the problems with this project is the cost of land.
In the type of housing the Legion was interested in providing there was absolutely no advantage in owning the land. If the federal government wanted to hold the land in title and provide it free of charge, it would have been acceptable. Let me tell you, Madam Speaker, the federal government owns a great deal of land. An inventory was taken a couple of years ago and it turned out it had land it did not even know about. In the province of Quebec the federal government started to sell land, and then when it looked at the situation closely it reconsidered and decided to hold that land. The federal government owns a considerable amount of land in every major city and it is costing money to maintain it. The government has no use for it at the moment and is holding it for future development.
One of the best things the government could do would be to provide federally owned land to organizations that want to provide accommodation for the people they are concerned with, at the lowest possible cost. The minister has said that this bill will assist the veterans, but I doubt that. I was shocked to hear the Minister for Veterans Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) delegate his responsibility to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) today. In doing so he gave the veterans absolutely nothing and took from them a long established program which, in my opinion, could have provided some advantages for them in the area of housing.
It would be easy for the government to provide land to interested organizations that could, as the hon. member for Broadview suggested, either pay the municipal taxes, which may be 4 per cent, or pay the government a dollar for it and let the government pay the taxes. In those cases where agencies or organizations are willing to provide the time, effort and labour, I think we should co-operate to ensure housing at a cost people can afford.
I understand that in the city of Toronto one of the major elements in the cost of housing is the price of land. I discussed this with one of my sons who lives there and was shocked when he indicated that a building lot costs about $25,000. I looked in the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star and saw that he was right. Not too long ago you could get a house for that price.
There is not much sense in promoting home ownership for people in a low income bracket if it is going to cost them 50 per cent of their wages. They would be better off to move into totally publicly supported housing and go on welfare. Of course many people are doing just that. It is not only the native population that we have neglected in this country. We have also neglected 25 percent of the rest of the population who are in the low wage bracket and are faced with the high cost of housing.
I can see no reason why the Minister of State for Urban Affairs would not be willing to take ownership of the land that rests with the Minister of Public Works in many
National Housing Act
municipalities, and designate it for low rental housing to be provided by other agencies.
The Legion in Haleybury started a project to provide its members with accommodation at a reasonable price. It worked hard on this but it is now in difficulty because of escalating costs and because we have not been providing the veterans with matching increases. The Legion is now asking the Ontario Housing Corporation to take the project over from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The minister has not shown any initiative in the field of public housing, but at least he could provide land at cost and so enable organizations to establish non-profit housing for people who are desperately in need.
Members who represent small communities are aware of the goodwill that exists in them and the desire of people to organize their time and efforts to develop non-profit housing for those who need it. I think the hon. member for Broadview is right when he says we could make land available to organizations on a lease basis for 4 per cent, or for a dollar, or even free of charge. Let us not give the kind of advantage that is in this bill to the big contractors, the friends of the minister, who are going to build houses. Because they get 1.8 per cent of the total cost they are going to raise the money to build houses? They have previously never built houses unless they got 15 per cent or 20 per cent.
A community spirit has to be developed in this country, Madam Speaker, and one way to do this is to allow organizations, willing to give their time, and sometimes money, to develop housing that is suitable for people and will provide a better standard of living for those who are not now able to afford decent housing. Anything else will not bring credit to the minister and, worse than that, will not build houses.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was most interested to hear the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Broadview effectively support the provision which calls for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to own land and retain title to it; that, of course, means for the people of Canada to own it and retain title to it.
The point that there are times when the consideration should be one dollar or 1 per cent is something I accept. The hon. member for Broadview asked me to stand up and say that. It is something I accept. There are other circumstances where it may not be applicable. It means the option for a non-profit group will be whichever suits them best. If it were limited to 4 per cent and the land was worth $1,000, naturally at $40 per year that is the option they would take. That would not be so bad, and it may be the right way to do it.
If the result is not economic rent, perhaps we are not going about this in the right way. If these people are getting the economic rent anyway, then they are depriving other non-profit groups, other sectors, other low income people of those funds. They might help in a particular development, but it might be unjust to let them take advantage of such programs if there are not sufficient

March 25, 1975
National Housing Act
funds for others. The land may be charged at $1 per year, or the rate may be 1 per cent, although I suggest in most cases it will be under 4 per cent. In some situations the interest rate may be 4 per cent, 5 per cent or 6 per cent. I think we must reserve our rights, otherwise we should give an unfair advantage to one group at the expense of another.
The intention is to give the non-profit or co-operative groups the right to the option. That is what we are trying to do in all our programs. We want to give people options which were never available to them before. As I say, we are trying to provide young people and low income people with the sort of option they have not had so far.
If the 10 per cent forgiveness allowance is not enough to cover the cost of the land, we can go further, buy that land and lease it back to these people at a low rent, to make certain that rents are maintained at a low level.

motion No. 5:
That Bill C-46, an Act to amend the National Housing Act, be amended in Clause 13:
(a)	by striking out lines 41 to 48 at page 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"qualified owner,"
(b)	by striking out line 12 at page 7 and substituting the following therefor:
"(l)(b) where the loan was made at a".
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the last motion I shall move. The hon. member for Winnipeg North suggests that if I can persuade the government to accept this amendment, I shall be as successful as if I had persuaded Paul to change his mind on the road to Damascus.
In 1973 the minister then responsible for housing, who now is the Minister of National Revenue, introduced Bill C-133 providing for the Assisted Home Ownership Program. He was proud of that program and thought great things would come of it. It was to come under the aegis of Central Mortgage and Housing. In 1974 the government acquired 4,000 existing homes under that program and built 16,000 additional homes. Its record was quite good. The program made available 20,000 homes to low and moderate income people at reduced rents.
We thought that was a fair start for the AHOP program. Then the present Minister of State for Urban Affairs came on the scene, and things changed. He said the AHOP program would apply only to new housing. The program was restricted, but the minister was proud of the funds which had been allocated for it. Now, by producing the present amending bill, he is abandoning the AHOP program. The government is not to be involved. It is saying to private builders that if a purchaser is approved by an approved lender for a mortgage under the AHOP program, the government will give that purchaser a subsidy with which to pay the higher interest rate he must pay on the mortgage.
When the government controlled the AHOP program the purchaser paid a rate of interest fixed by the government. Now that approved lenders have entered the picture, interest rates will increase, probably up to 10.5 per cent. In effect the minister says, "I will give the purchaser a subsidy; he may pass it on to the lending institution." In other words the minister says, "I will give a subsidy to the lending institutions; the government will pay it to the purchaser, or mortgagor, who will pass it on to the mortgagee."
We say that is wrong, that the government should control AHOP because the lower interest rate represents an advantage to the buyer. If the government were to assume greater responsibility, it could exercise greater control over the administration, over building standards and over maintenance.
Not content with giving a subsidy directly to financial institutions, the parliamentary secretary moved an amendment in committee which said that private insurance companies should handle the mortgage insurance on these homes. So, what do we have? The government wants
March 25, 1975

to subsidize the financial institutions, and the parliamentary secretary wants private insurance companies to handle the mortgage insurance on these homes. I suggest that when the government was more directly responsible for the AHOP program, CMHC controlled building standards and the matter of mortgage insurance. There are tremendous sums of money in the mortgage insurance fund-I think over $400 million at the moment. Claims against the fund are minimal. I therefore think that it is logical to ask CMHC to handle the mortgage insurance fund.
What does the minister do? What do the financial institutions do? They say they want a subsidy on any AHOP mortgage, as well as mortgage insurance. If that is not getting it two ways, I do not know what is. Unfortunately it fits in with the philosophy the minister has expressed on different occasions. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) says it is the trickle down theory, the trickle down to the financial institutions such as the banks, the trust companies, insurance companies and private insurers.
The minister put it in a rather coarse but meaningful way when he said it was more bang for the buck. It is more bang for the buck to the lending institutions, developers and builders. That is really what he is talking about.
If assisted ownership is to apply to low income people, they should have the benefit of any subsidies paid by the government in order to reduce their mortgage interest rates, and they should have the protection with regard to mortgage insurance.
When this program was devised in the first instance in 1973, we told the present Minister of National Revenue that it really applied to the middle income group and not the low income group. They said we were wrong. It is fair to show that it goes to the middle income group.
The best example of this is the city of Toronto. Michael Dennis, housing commissioner for the city of Toronto, wrote a report which was published in February of this year showing what the AHOP program has done for the city of Toronto. What has happened? Not one house was built in the city of Toronto under the AHOP program. In Metro Toronto, which includes the suburbs, only 191 were built. I brought this to the attention of the minister when we were in committee. He replied that there were 1,716 built in Metro Toronto. He said they have gone as far as West Hill. West Hill is half way to Oshawa. I have never heard of it being included in Metro Toronto. This was the feeble answer of the minister and his officials with regard to the AHOP program. The AHOP program should help people in the lower income group.

The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling) says it should also help people in the rural areas. I agree 100 per cent. It should help people in rural areas, small towns and big cities. We said that. It has helped people in small towns.
National Housing Act
The minister has said that in order to qualify for the program you must have a certain income, and the home must be within a certain price range. He pointed out in committee that under the AHOP program the average income of a purchaser is $9,336. May I add that this really only applied to those in the small towns, villages and rural areas. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka can tell me with a nod that that is a big income for a person in a small town to make in order to qualify under the AHOP program. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) can tell me that the income a person needs to qualify in the city of Toronto must be very large.
Not one house was built under the AHOP program in the city of Toronto. Only 191 houses were built on the metro scene. It is about time the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stopped looking after the oil companies and started looking after people in the city of Toronto. I have never seen a minister who is so sympathetic to the oil companies and so unsympathetic to the people of his area with regard to public housing and the AHOP scheme.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, most important-and what this bill does not deal with-is the major shift in federal housing policy that is being imposed by the CMHC capital spending budget. The capital spending budget determines government policy. It allocates the amount of moneys that will go to cost-shared programs with the provinces and those that will go directly to unilateral federal programs.
There is a massive shift away from the socially assisted programs the federal government has developed with the provinces and municipalities over recent years to programs such as AHOP, which is the one being dealt with in this clause, programs which are controlled and operated out of Ottawa primarily for those in the moderate income range. Directly traceable to the capital spending budget of CMHC is the two-pronged shift in government housing policy-first, a cut-back in cost shared programs with the provinces and municipalities in favour of the theory that Ottawa should have control, and second, a move away from the long established role of government to assist with public housing to a new and questionable role of supplying mortgage moneys at privileged rates to those in the moderate income bracket.
One is almost inclined to suspect that these major policy shifts are designed primarily to satisfy the building urge of the president of CMHC. Certainly they are arrived at in isolation from the needs of those most closely related to the housing scene-governments at the municipal and provincial levels.
This shift in housing policy, as I pointed out to the minister the other day, is directly accountable for a shortfall this year of some 4,000 senior citizens units in the province of Ontario alone, and a similar situation is developing in most of the other provinces. My colleagues from Saskatchewan and British Columbia have already mentioned this situation.
Earlier today the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) decided to set the matter straight by pointing to the great involvement of the government in the field of public housing and the shortcoming on the part of the government of Ontario to match it. Obviously he had not been looking at recent figures, or even consulting with his colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson). For the record, Mr. Speaker, the Postmaster

General may be interested to know that in 1973 the federal government's allocation to Ontario for socially assisted housing was $130 million, in 1974 it was $78 million, and in 1975 it has been set at a mere $50.4 million whereas Ontario has a take-up capacity of some $400 million, which has been encouraged over the past number of years by programs on which the federal government has now defaulted.
The capital spending budget of CMHC has gone up just 12.4 per cent this year while at the same time Ontario, recognizing the housing emergency, has increased its spending on social housing programs by 50 per cent. I mention these figures so that the Postmaster General and others can be better informed on what is taking place in Ontario.
This situation is very serious, Mr. Speaker. The decrease in funds to Ontario and to other provinces for socially assisted housing as directed by the federal government illustrates the point clearly. The federal government has shifted its priorities in residential construction through manipulation of the CMHC capital spending budget, a budget which heretofore there has been no opportunity to review.
Members of the New Democratic Party have been trying to utilize the present bill to come to grips with the shift in government policy. I do not believe this bill is the vehicle to achieve that goal, Mr. Speaker. The most direct way to ensure this is to let us have the capital spending budget of CMHC for examination in detail. In committee on March 20 the minister assured me this would be done. Tonight I would like further assurance from the minister as to when we will have a reference of the CMHC capital budget from the House to committee. I should like him to tell us when this will come about, because only then can we have a proper examination of the reasons for and objectives of the shifts in government housing policy.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that there be much longer forward planning on the part of the federal government to meet the housing needs of the country. Certainly if the government is to honour its commitment to the cost sharing programs it is imperative that that be done. At present the provinces and municipalities are limited in their planning by the way in which they are presented with a year to year allocation of federal funding into which they have had no input, and about which they have not been consulted.
The government must spell out its priorities clearly for longer periods and put an end to the stop-start approach it has had to these programs. There should be some immediate steps to establish a formula for a period of at least three years so that the provinces, municipalities and other groups can undertake and initiate programs with the confidence that they will be able to continue them once they are started, with help from the federal government.
There is no overall, coherent approach to the housing needs of the country. There is no long term planning and no co-ordination with transportation policy, immigration policy, and land use policy. Rather, the minister is content to rely on faith and prayers for a sum he says will be in the vicinity of $1 billion this year from private mortgage lenders, and as well on a multiplicity of restrictive programs such as the one he introduced today for veterans.

The hon. member knows that the House often depends on his experience and good advice, and I would not want to engage in a procedural debate. I did express an opinion as to the relationship between one Standing Order and another. At the same time, however,

the House seemed to be ready to come to some kind of agreement and I would invite members to find an immediate solution to the situation which faces us. If hon. members have a solution I would invite them to express it to the Chair.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I still hold the view on the point of procedure, with respect, that the power to proceed to an additional stage cannot be any greater on extended sittings than it was before ten o'clock. I would suggest that we proceed to pass the motion and, if we get through report stage and the government wants to proceed to third reading and somebody objects, then the Chair would have to make a ruling at that stage.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I understand the difficulty that faces Your Honour. I have read the subparagraph to mean that we can deal with more than one stage because this section seems fairly clear on that point. On the other hand, it is a very difficult point and I do not think we want to settle it tonight. As far as I am concerned, if we can dispose of report stage I would hope that we would have the co-operation of all members to agree to go to third reading tonight as well, even though this motion I have made might not technically cover that.
